content_voiceover: This slide presents two board style practice questions. Question four asks which statement is wrong about prognostic factors in adult ALL. The answer is C. Option C states that early T cell precursor, or ETP, ALL is a poor prognostic subtype for which stem cell transplant is usually unable to improve outcome, and this is the incorrect statement, because although ETP ALL was traditionally considered high risk, allogeneic stem cell transplantation in first remission can actually improve outcomes in this subgroup, so transplant is not futile as the option implies. The other options are all true: advanced age and high white count are adverse factors, high WBC in T-ALL only matters above one hundred times ten to the ninth per liter, early blast persistence after seven days of induction reflects steroid resistance, and MRD negativity after consolidation predicts durable remission. Question six asks which description of a novel ALL agent is wrong, and the answer is B. Option B incorrectly states that clofarabine was approved by the FDA, misspelled as FAD, for both pediatric and adult relapsed refractory ALL. In fact, clofarabine's approval was limited to pediatric patients aged one to twenty one years with relapsed or refractory ALL after at least two prior regimens, not adults. The other options describing nelarabine for T-ALL, inotuzumab for CD22 positive B-ALL, and blinatumomab's survival benefit are accurate.
keypoints: Question four answer C, ETP-ALL is poor prognosis but transplant CAN still improve outcome, not futile
High WBC only adversely affects T-ALL survival above one hundred times ten to ninth per liter
Question six answer B, clofarabine FDA approval is pediatric only, ages one to twenty one, not adults
Nelarabine approved for T-ALL and T-lymphoblastic lymphoma; inotuzumab approved for CD22 positive B-ALL
keypoint_voiceover: For these two questions, remember that ETP-ALL, despite being high risk, can still benefit from allogeneic transplant, making option C wrong in question four. And remember clofarabine's FDA approval is restricted to pediatric relapsed refractory ALL, not adults, which makes option B wrong in question six.
